questions.stem: Which of these relations is a function?
questions.explanation: A function pairs each x-value with exactly one y-value, and repeating a y-value (2 appears twice) is allowed. The set with (1, 2) and (1, 3) pairs x = 1 with two y-values, and the circle and x = y² each fail the vertical line test.

questions.stem: The vertical line test shows that a relation is a function when:
options: every vertical line meets its graph exactly once
its graph passes through the origin
every vertical line meets its graph at most once
every horizontal line meets its graph at most once
questions.explanation: A function gives at most one output for each input, so no vertical line may cut the graph twice. The horizontal line test is a different test: it decides whether a function is one-to-one. Exactly once is too strong, because a vertical line outside the domain meets the graph nowhere.

questions.stem: What is the maximal (implied) domain of f(x) = √(x − 3)?
questions.explanation: The square root needs x − 3 ≥ 0, so x ≥ 3, and x = 3 itself is allowed because √0 = 0. The open interval (3, ∞) wrongly leaves out that endpoint.

questions.stem: What is the maximal domain of f(x) = 1/(x + 2)?
questions.explanation: The only forbidden value is the one that makes the denominator zero: x + 2 = 0 gives x = −2. Excluding 2 is the sign slip, and excluding 0 belongs to y = 1/x before it was translated.

questions.stem: For f: [−1, 2] → R, f(x) = x², what is the range of f?
questions.explanation: The domain includes x = 0, where x² takes its least value 0, and the greatest value is at x = 2, giving 4. Substituting only the endpoints gives 1 and 4, which misses the turning point inside the domain.

questions.stem: For f: R → R, f(x) = x² + 1, what is the co-domain of f?
questions.explanation: The co-domain is the set written after the arrow in the function's specification, here R. The range is the set of values actually reached, which is [1, ∞). The two are easily confused because both describe outputs.

questions.stem: If f(x) = 3 − 2x, what is f(a + 1)?
questions.explanation: Replace x with the whole of a + 1: f(a + 1) = 3 − 2(a + 1) = 3 − 2a − 2 = 1 − 2a. Writing 5 − 2a comes from treating −2 × 1 as +2.

questions.stem: A relation is given by the table x: 1, 2, 2, 3 and y: 4, 5, 6, 7. Why is it not a function?
options: The y-values increase steadily as x increases
No y-value appears in the table more than once
The x-value 2 is paired with two different y-values
The y-values are all different from one another
questions.explanation: A function must give each input one output, and here x = 2 gives both 5 and 6. Having all y-values different is no barrier: many functions, such as y = x + 3, do exactly that.

questions.stem: The graph of y = f⁻¹(x) is the reflection of the graph of y = f(x) in which line?
questions.explanation: Finding an inverse swaps the coordinates of every point, and swapping (a, b) to (b, a) is reflection in the line y = x. Reflection in an axis changes the sign of one coordinate instead.

questions.stem: The point (2, 5) lies on the graph of a one-to-one function f. Which point lies on the graph of f⁻¹?
questions.explanation: The inverse reverses the input and output, so (2, 5) becomes (5, 2). The point (1/2, 1/5) confuses the inverse function with the reciprocal.

questions.stem: What is the inverse function of f(x) = 2x + 6?
questions.explanation: Swap x and y to get x = 2y + 6, then solve: y = (x − 6)/2. Writing x/2 − 6 undoes the steps in the wrong order, and 1/(2x + 6) is the reciprocal, not the inverse.

questions.stem: Which of these functions has an inverse function?
questions.explanation: An inverse function exists only for a one-to-one function. Restricting x² to [0, ∞) keeps just the right half of the parabola, which passes the horizontal line test. Over [−2, 2] the values x = −1 and x = 1 still share the output 1.

questions.stem: If f(x) = x³ + 1, what is the value of f⁻¹(9)?
questions.explanation: f⁻¹(9) is the input that gives 9, so solve x³ + 1 = 9: x³ = 8 and x = 2. The value 730 is f(9), which is the function applied rather than undone.

questions.stem: f: [1, 5] → R, f(x) = 2x − 1. What are the domain and range of f⁻¹?
questions.explanation: The range of f is [f(1), f(5)] = [1, 9]. The inverse swaps domain and range, so f⁻¹ has domain [1, 9] and range [1, 5]. Keeping the domain [1, 5] forgets that the swap applies to the sets as well as the points.

questions.stem: f: [1, ∞) → R, f(x) = (x − 1)². What is the rule of f⁻¹?
questions.explanation: Swapping gives x = (y − 1)², so y − 1 = ±√x. The range of f⁻¹ must be the domain of f, [1, ∞), so the positive root is taken and y = 1 + √x. Taking 1 − √x would give values below 1, which f never has as inputs.

questions.stem: What is the inverse function of f(x) = 1/(x − 2) + 3, x ≠ 2?
questions.explanation: Swap to x = 1/(y − 2) + 3, so x − 3 = 1/(y − 2) and y = 1/(x − 3) + 2. The asymptotes x = 2 and y = 3 swap to x = 3 and y = 2, which is a quick check. Subtracting 2 at the end reverses the last step's sign.

questions.stem: The graph of a polynomial function has a stationary point of inflection at x = 2. Which statement is true?
options: The gradient is zero at x = 2 and has the same sign on both sides
The gradient is zero at x = 2 and changes sign there
The graph must cross the x-axis at the point where x = 2
The gradient of the graph is undefined at the point x = 2
questions.explanation: A stationary point of inflection is flat for an instant, but the graph keeps rising (or keeps falling) through it. A gradient that changes sign marks a turning point, a local maximum or minimum.

questions.stem: A graph shows a company's total sales over a year. Sales always rise. The rate of increase falls until June, then grows for the rest of the year. What is the feature at June?
options: A local minimum, where the sales stop falling and begin to rise
A local maximum, where the sales reach their highest value
A vertical asymptote, where the sales increase without bound
A point of inflection, where the rate of increase is least
questions.explanation: Sales never fall, so there is no turning point; what changes is how steeply they rise. The gradient falls to its smallest value at June and then grows, so the graph changes from concave down to concave up there, which marks a point of inflection.

questions.stem: The temperature in a Ballarat backyard rises all morning, levels off for an instant at 21 °C at noon, then keeps rising until 3 pm. What feature does the graph show at noon?
questions.explanation: The graph is flat at noon but rises both before and after, so the gradient is zero without changing sign. A local maximum would need the temperature to fall after noon.

questions.stem: What are the asymptotes of the graph of y = 1/x?
questions.explanation: 1/x is undefined at x = 0 and approaches 0 as x grows large in either direction, so both axes are asymptotes. The graph is symmetric about y = x but never approaches that line.

questions.stem: What are the asymptotes of the graph of y = 2/(x − 3) + 1?
questions.explanation: The graph of y = 1/x is translated 3 units right and 1 unit up, so the asymptotes move to x = 3 and y = 1. The dilation factor 2 stretches the graph but does not move any asymptote.

questions.stem: What is the range of y = 1/(x + 1)² − 4?
questions.explanation: 1/(x + 1)² is always positive and never zero, so y is always greater than −4 but never equals it. Including −4 forgets that the horizontal asymptote is approached and never reached.

questions.stem: Which of these functions has maximal domain R?
questions.explanation: Every real number has a real cube root, including negative numbers: the cube root of −8 is −2. The square root needs x ≥ 2, and the two reciprocal functions are undefined at x = 2.

questions.stem: The graph of y = −√(x − 2) + 3 has which endpoint and range?
questions.explanation: The graph of y = √x is reflected in the x-axis, then moved 2 right and 3 up, so it starts at (2, 3) and heads downward. The reflection is what makes the range (−∞, 3] rather than [3, ∞).

questions.stem: For 0 < x < 1, which of these has the greatest value?
questions.explanation: For a number between 0 and 1, raising it to a higher power makes it smaller, and a root makes it larger: at x = 0.25, √x = 0.5, x² = 0.0625 and x³ ≈ 0.016. The order reverses for x > 1.

questions.stem: Which statement describes the graph of y = 1/x²?
options: It passes through the origin and lies above the x-axis
It lies below the x-axis for negative values of x
It lies above the x-axis and is symmetric about the y-axis
It lies in the first and third quadrants and is symmetric about the origin
questions.explanation: Squaring makes x² positive for every x ≠ 0, so y is always positive and the same for x and −x. The first and third quadrants describe y = 1/x, whose sign follows the sign of x.

questions.stem: A truncus y = a/(x − 2)² − 1 passes through the point (3, 1). What is the value of a?
questions.explanation: Substitute x = 3: a/1² − 1 = 1, so a = 2. Getting 1 comes from forgetting to add the 1 across, and the graph then passes through (3, 0) instead.

questions.stem: A hyperbola y = a/(x − 1) + 2 passes through the origin. What is the value of a?
questions.explanation: At (0, 0): 0 = a/(0 − 1) + 2, so −a + 2 = 0 and a = 2. The answer −2 comes from treating 0 − 1 as +1; with a = −2 the graph would pass through (0, 4).

questions.stem: Where is the stationary point of inflection of y = −2(x + 1)³ + 4?
questions.explanation: y = x³ has its stationary point of inflection at the origin. Here it is translated 1 left and 4 up, so the point is (−1, 4). The factor −2 reflects and dilates the graph but does not move this point.

questions.stem: What is the range of y = 3 − 1/x?
questions.explanation: 1/x takes every real value except 0, so 3 − 1/x takes every value except 3. The horizontal asymptote y = 3 is the excluded value; 0 is excluded only for y = 1/x itself.

questions.stem: What is the maximal domain of y = √(4 − 2x) + 1?
questions.explanation: The square root needs 4 − 2x ≥ 0, so 2x ≤ 4 and x ≤ 2. The interval [2, ∞) comes from forgetting that the negative coefficient of x points the graph to the left.

questions.stem: Where does the graph of y = 2(x − 1)^(1/3) − 2 cross the x-axis?
questions.explanation: Set y = 0: 2(x − 1)^(1/3) = 2, so (x − 1)^(1/3) = 1, x − 1 = 1 and x = 2. The answer x = 9 comes from forgetting to divide by 2 first, which gives a cube root of 2 and x − 1 = 8.

questions.stem: At x = 2, the graph of y = (x − 2)²(x + 1):
options: touches the x-axis at a turning point
crosses the x-axis with non-zero gradient
has a stationary point of inflection
questions.explanation: A repeated factor (x − 2)² does not change sign, so the graph comes down to the axis and turns back. A factor cubed, such as (x − 2)³, would give a stationary point of inflection instead.

questions.stem: For y = −2x³ + x, what happens to y as x → ∞?
questions.explanation: For large x the leading term −2x³ dominates, and it becomes a large negative number. A positive leading coefficient would send y to ∞ instead.

questions.stem: What is the y-intercept of y = (x − 1)(x + 2)(x − 3)?
questions.explanation: Set x = 0: (−1)(2)(−3) = 6. The two negative factors multiply to a positive, which is where the answer −6 goes wrong.

questions.stem: At the point (2, 0), the graph of y = x(x − 2)³ has:
options: a local minimum touching the axis
a local maximum touching the axis
questions.explanation: The factor (x − 2)³ is odd-powered, so the graph crosses the axis, and because the power is 3 it flattens as it crosses. A squared factor would give a turning point touching the axis.

questions.stem: A quartic with a positive leading coefficient touches the x-axis at x = −2 and crosses it at x = 1 and x = 3. Which rule could it have?
questions.explanation: A touch point at x = −2 needs the squared factor (x + 2)², and crossings at 1 and 3 need the single factors (x − 1) and (x − 3). The rule with (x − 2)² has every intercept's sign reversed, and the negative one has the wrong leading coefficient.

questions.stem: How many x-intercepts can the graph of a cubic polynomial function have?
questions.explanation: A cubic heads to opposite infinities at its two ends, so it must cross the x-axis at least once. Two intercepts are possible when one is a touch point, as in y = x²(x − 1).

questions.stem: Which function has a graph that is symmetric about the y-axis?
questions.explanation: A polynomial containing only even powers gives the same value at x and −x, so its graph is symmetric about the y-axis. y = x³ − x and y = 1/x are symmetric about the origin instead, and (x − 1)² is symmetric about x = 1.

questions.stem: Where does the graph of y = (x² − 4)² meet the x-axis?
options: It touches at x = −2 and x = 2
It crosses at x = −2 and x = 2
questions.explanation: (x² − 4)² = (x − 2)²(x + 2)², so each intercept comes from a squared factor and the graph touches the axis at both. At x = 0 the value is 16, which is the y-intercept, not an x-intercept.

questions.stem: For which values of x is x³ > x²?
questions.explanation: x³ − x² = x²(x − 1). The factor x² is never negative, so the difference is positive only when x − 1 > 0 and x ≠ 0, that is x > 1. For negative x, x³ is negative while x² is positive.

questions.stem: An open box made from a 10 cm square sheet has volume V(x) = x(10 − 2x)², where x cm is the side of the squares cut from each corner. What is the modelling domain?
questions.explanation: The cut must be positive, and the base side 10 − 2x must also be positive, so x < 5. The rule is defined for any x, but (0, 10) allows cuts larger than half the sheet, which is physically impossible.
